headline: 2.2 trillion BDT: S Alam Group laundered money via hundi and trade
summary: A BFIU report reveals how the group took loans from banks and smuggled funds abroad through international trade and hundi channels.
details: The Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU) has reported that S Alam Group laundered approximately 2.2 trillion BDT.
According to the report, the group obtained loans from various banks, both in their own name and through proxy accounts.
These funds were then smuggled out of the country using international trade mechanisms and hundi channels.
The scale of the loot and money laundering operation is one of the largest in the country's history.
caption:
2.2 trillion BDT laundered. How did S Alam Group move such a massive sum out of Bangladesh?

The Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU) has reported that S Alam Group laundered approximately 2.2 trillion BDT.

According to the report, the group obtained loans from various banks, both in their own name and through proxy accounts.

These funds were then smuggled out of the country using international trade mechanisms and hundi channels.

The scale of the loot and money laundering operation is one of the largest in the country's history.

headline_marked: High Court issues rule to [[ensure minimum education for UP chairmen]]
headline: High Court issues rule to ensure minimum education for UP chairmen
summary: The court is questioning why a minimum educational qualification, such as a graduate degree, should not be mandated for Union Parishad chairman candidates.
details: The High Court has issued a rule asking the government to explain why a minimum educational qualification should not be mandated for candidates contesting the Union Parishad (UP) chairman post.
A bench comprising Justice Ahmed Sohel and Justice Fatema Anwar issued the rule following a writ petition filed by two Supreme Court lawyers, Md. Tanveer Ahmed Khan and Kazi Ferdousul Hasan.

The petition argues that Section 26 of the Local Government (Union Parishad) Act 2009 currently allows individuals to run for chairman without any educational requirements, which they claim is unconstitutional.

The lawyers argue that this lack of qualification is inconsistent with the Village Court Act, as UP chairmen hold judicial powers to impose fines of up to 3 lakh BDT, similar to second-class judicial magistrates.

They further state that while judicial magistrates must have a law degree to be appointed, it is contradictory that UP chairmen, who exercise similar financial penalties, have no educational requirements.
The court has directed the Local Government Secretary, Law Secretary, and the Chief Election Commissioner to respond to the rule within four weeks.
caption:
Should UP chairmen be required to have a graduate degree? The High Court is now questioning the current law.

The High Court has issued a rule asking the government to explain why a minimum educational qualification should not be mandated for candidates contesting the Union Parishad (UP) chairman post.

A bench comprising Justice Ahmed Sohel and Justice Fatema Anwar issued the rule following a writ petition filed by two Supreme Court lawyers, Md. Tanveer Ahmed Khan and Kazi Ferdousul Hasan.

The petition argues that Section 26 of the Local Government (Union Parishad) Act 2009 currently allows individuals to run for chairman without any educational requirements, which they claim is unconstitutional.

The lawyers argue that this lack of qualification is inconsistent with the Village Court Act, as UP chairmen hold judicial powers to impose fines of up to 3 lakh BDT, similar to second-class judicial magistrates.

They further state that while judicial magistrates must have a law degree to be appointed, it is contradictory that UP chairmen, who exercise similar financial penalties, have no educational requirements.

The court has directed the Local Government Secretary, Law Secretary, and the Chief Election Commissioner to respond to the rule within four weeks.
